doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

chapter: Cecil Taylor and the new music
title: Taylor's sidemen and partners
summary: Playing with Taylor was hard; Sonny Murray and Jimmy Lyons grew under him, and the Mary Lou Williams and Max Roach records.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Did you hear him with various sidemen and if so did you observe anything watching the sidemen that reflected the challenge of playing with Cecil Taylor?

Yeah, not everybody could do it, and not just sideman also like co-partners. I mean you know if you listen to the Mary Lou Williams/Cecil Taylor record they’re not always in accord. Or the Max Roach one, where they — certainly they had no trouble finding a common rhythm but the question of whose voice would be on top was an issue. But there is great music on both of those recordings. There are points at which they’d come together brilliantly. But as for the sidemen he basically developed musicians. Sonny Murray for example, who actually is a more important drummer than is generally acknowledged. Sonny I saw grow through his work with Cecil, you could see it, see his improvement. And his sense of finding out what Cecil needed from the drums, which was not propulsion as Cecil certainly had enough of that, but more of a pattern of, what am I looking for — a more of an impulse that could just sort of work in concert with the piano. So you could see Jimmy Lyons for example, a very, very good musician who should be noted more. Jimmy Lyons was able to play a more standard kind of a sound but would have the rhythmic capability as well as the fluidity not to get stuck from bar line to bar line but to just flow across it all and go wherever Cecil took him, still at the same time remaining very accessible. So yes, he basically developed people.
